tamid-27b-10-11.note: Rav Safra was in a bathroom when Rabbi Abba came by and coughed to ask whether he might come in. Rav Safra told him: Enter, Master. When Rav Safra came out, Rabbi Abba rebuked him: you have never been to Seir, yet you have learned the ways of Seir. Did the mishna not teach that a closed door shows someone is inside, meaning that no one should go in while another person is there?
tamid-27b-10-11.why: The mishna describes a dignified bathroom in the Temple whose closed door showed it was in use. The Gemara then defends Rav Safra: he feared Rabbi Abba's health would be at risk if he had to hold back.

people.name: Rav Safra
people.about: Invites Rabbi Abba into the bathroom while he is inside.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: Enters at Rav Safra's invitation and then rebukes him for it.

terms.meaning: The land of the Edomites; here a byword for people who behave immodestly.

tamid-27b-15-15.note: A man drank water and, without pouring some out first, handed the cup to his student. The student was a fastidious person and would not drink from it, and he died of thirst. At that time the Sages ruled that a person should not drink water and give the rest to his student unless he first pours some of it out.
tamid-27b-15-15.why: Rav and Rav Huna have just told their sons to pour out a little water before passing the cup to a student; this baraita gives the incident behind that advice. Rav Ashi draws from it that a student who pours out water in front of his teacher is not being disrespectful.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Concludes that a student may pour out water in front of his teacher without disrespect.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.

tamid-28a-8-8.note: Two priests were tied as they raced up the altar ramp. One of them shoved the other, and his leg was broken. When the court saw that people were coming into danger, they ruled that the ashes would be removed from the altar only by lottery.
tamid-28a-8-8.why: The Gemara is reconciling two clauses of the mishna: in one, the first priest ready removes the ashes; in the other, a lottery decides. Abaye says the first describes practice before the lottery was enacted, and this incident is why it was enacted.

terms.meaning: The first Temple task each morning, clearing ashes from the altar; priests competed for the honor.
The sloping walkway priests climbed to reach the top of the altar.

tamid-31b-14-14.note: Alexander of Macedon put ten questions to the Elders of the Negev: about distances, the order of creation (they declined to say whether light or darkness came first), who is wise, mighty and rich, how to live and how to die. When they said that even Satan is sometimes victorious, he threatened to execute them; they replied that falsehood does not suit a king, and he dressed them in purple and gold chains. Using their advice to cross the Mountains of Darkness, he reached a town of women, who served him bread of gold, and he wrote on its gate that he had learned sense from women. At a spring he guessed it flowed from the Garden of Eden. One version says he reached its gate, was refused, and was given an eyeball that outweighed all his gold, until it was covered with dust.
tamid-31b-14-14.why: The Gemara has been explaining where the daily offerings were slaughtered by the position of the sun; Alexander's first question, answered from how hard it is to look at the sun at midday, ties the story to that discussion.

people.name: Alexander of Macedon
people.about: The king who questions the Elders of the Negev and goes on a campaign to Africa.

people.name: The Elders of the Negev
people.about: The Jewish Sages whom Alexander questions and who advise him.

people.name: The women of the town
people.about: The people of a town of women who talk Alexander out of fighting them.

terms.meaning: A dark mountain range that, the Elders said, blocked the way to Africa.
The garden of the first humans, here pictured as a real place whose gate only the righteous may enter.
In this text, a force that leads people to do what is clearly wrong.

tamid-32b-0-3.note: Alexander asked the women whether people eat bread of gold. They replied that if he only wanted bread, he had bread at home; that was not why he had come. On leaving, he wrote on the town gate: I, Alexander of Macedon, was a fool until I came to the land of Africa of women, and I learned sense from women. Later, eating salted fish by a spring, he smelled a fragrance and concluded the spring came from the Garden of Eden. Some say he followed it to Eden's gate and demanded entry; refused, he asked for something, and was given an eyeball that outweighed all his gold and silver. The Sages told him the human eye is never satisfied, and once he covered it with dirt, it balanced.
tamid-32b-0-3.why: This continues the Gemara's account of Alexander, which began with his questions to the Elders of the Negev and his march to Africa. After it, the Gemara adds a teaching that Gehenna lies beyond the Mountains of Darkness he crossed.

people.name: Alexander of Macedon
people.about: A king on campaign in Africa, who learns from a town of women and seeks entry to the Garden of Eden.

terms.meaning: Paradise, the garden of the first humans; here its gate is guarded and only the righteous may enter.
